traveler: Xuanzang (Chen Hui), the Master of the Law
title: Sixteen Years for the Scriptures: the Illegal Departure, Nalanda, and the Translation Bureau
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The House of Chen and the Monastery at Luoyang

stops.name: Chenhe village near Luoyang, the fourth son of the Chen
stops.date_confidence: year traditional; month and day unrecorded, and the birth name is given as Chen Hui in some sources and Chen Yi in others
stops.campa: In a village of Luozhou, a day's walk from Luoyang, a fourth son is born to the Chen family, officials and Confucian scholars four generations deep. They name him Chen Hui; some records give Chen Yi. His great-grandfather was a prefect, his grandfather taught in the imperial academy, and his father has withdrawn from office as the Sui begin to fail, raising his sons at home on the classics. The boy reads the Book of Filial Piety before anyone thinks to send him anywhere. His mother, the biographies say, has already dreamt him walking west in a white robe.
stops.quote: You are my son, where then are you going?
stops.quote_source: Huili, The Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Samuel Beal, Book I, pp. 10-11 (the mother's dream; his answer is given as 'I am going to seek for the Law')
suggested_refs: Chenhe village, Goushi, near Luoyang, the traditional birthplace
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Samuel Beal

stops.name: Luoyang, the novice at Jingtu Monastery
stops.date_confidence: attested to 611 for the move; the novice ordination at thirteen is dated by Huili and by Wikipedia, not by a document
stops.campa: His father dies, and the boy is taken to Jingtu Monastery in Luoyang, where his elder brother Changjie is already a monk. He follows the sutra lectures from the back of the hall and remembers what he hears. At thirteen an imperial commissioner examining candidates for the order finds him below the age of rule and admits him anyway, on the strength of his answers; he is ordained a novice and given the dharma name Xuanzang. Full ordination is still nine years off. He spends those years on the Nirvana Sutra and the Mahayana-samgraha, and on the places where their Chinese versions disagree.
suggested_refs: Jingtu Monastery, Luoyang, where the dharma name Xuanzang was conferred

stops.name: Chengdu, ordained at twenty
stops.date_confidence: attested: full bhiksu ordination in 622 at age twenty, both sources agreeing
stops.campa: The Sui dynasty comes apart, Luoyang is fought over, and the brothers leave it for Chang'an and then for Sichuan, where the war has not yet reached. In Chengdu the monasteries are crowded with refugee teachers from the whole collapsing empire, and Xuanzang studies under all of them, Abhidharma and the Mahayana treatises together. At twenty he takes the full bhiksu ordination. He hears one scripture explained in incompatible ways by masters nobody disputes, and cannot make the readings meet.
suggested_refs: The refugee monasteries of Chengdu during the Sui collapse

stops.name: Chang'an, the incomplete scriptures
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the date marks a process of study rather than an event
stops.campa: Back in the new Tang capital he takes up Sanskrit and works through the translations available in Chinese, comparing versions of one text against each other. The Yogacarabhumi in particular reaches him in fragments and in renderings that contradict one another, and no master in Chang'an can say which carries the original sense. He concludes that the question cannot be settled in China at all, because the settling copy is in India. He begins to plan a journey the Tang state does not permit its subjects to make.
stops.quote: The purpose of my journey is not to obtain personal offerings. It is because I regretted, in my country, the Buddhist doctrine was imperfect and the scriptures were incomplete.
stops.quote_source: Xuanzang, trans. Li Yung-hsi (1959), quoted in Wikipedia, 'Xuanzang'
suggested_refs: The competing Chinese recensions of the Yogacarabhumi-sastra before 629

stops.name: Chang'an, the petition refused
stops.date_confidence: disputed: traditional biographies give 627, modern scholarship generally 629, and the sources consulted do not resolve it
stops.campa: He petitions the court for a travel permit and is refused: the frontier is closed, the Turks are unsettled, and no subject may leave. He joins a party of famine refugees allowed out of the capital during a bad harvest and goes west with them, an outlaw from his first mile. He is twenty-seven. He has no permit and no interpreter, and no account of the road ahead except what stands in the books that sent him. Nobody at court is told, and the refugees he walks out with do not know who he is.
stops.quote: Having many doubts, I wish to go and find out the truth, and so I decided to travel to the West at the risk of my life
stops.quote_source: Xuanzang, trans. Li Yung-hsi (1959), quoted in Wikipedia, 'Xuanzang'
suggested_refs: The Tang edict closing the western frontier to private travel
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: Liangzhou, the sermon that betrays him
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Huili gives the sequence but not the month
stops.campa: He travels the corridor through Qinzhou and Lanzhou, crossing the Yellow River at the frontier garrison, and reaches Liangzhou, the last large town of Tang authority. Merchants from the western kingdoms are wintering there; he is asked to preach and does, to crowds large enough that word reaches the governor, who holds the emperor's order barring travel west and instructs him to turn back to Chang'an. Two local monks hide him and move him out by night. From here he travels in darkness and lies up by day.
suggested_refs: Liangzhou, modern Wuwei, terminus of lawful Tang travel in 629
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: Guazhou, the warrant torn up
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the episode is Huili's and has no independent corroboration
stops.campa: At Guazhou the arrest warrant catches up with him, sent ahead by the governor of Liangzhou and naming him as a fugitive. The prefect Li Chang reads it, looks at the monk in front of him, and asks him plainly whether he is the man. Xuanzang says he is. Li Chang tears the document up in his presence and tells him to leave quickly. His horse dies here; a foreign guide is found, and an old red horse that has crossed the desert fifteen times is bought to carry what the dead one carried.
stops.quote: The Master ought to speak the truth, and your disciple will make some plan for you to escape.
stops.quote_source: Li Chang, governor of Kwa-chow, in Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal, Book I, p. 14
suggested_refs: The imperial warrant for Xuanzang's arrest, destroyed at Guazhou
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: The Jade Gate, crossed by night
stops.date_confidence: 629 attested; the Tang-era Jade Gate stood near Guazhou on the Hulu river, not at the abandoned Han ruins near Dunhuang, and its exact site is identified by inference
stops.campa: The Jade Gate is the last gate. Beyond it stand five beacon towers, a day apart, each garrisoned, each holding the only water for a hundred li. The guide Shi Pantuo brings him over the Hulu river by night, cutting the crossing with felled wood, and then loses his nerve: he cannot follow a fugitive past the towers without losing his own head. Xuanzang gives him the horse and provisions and lets him go, and rides on alone into country where every well is watched by men ordered to stop him.
stops.quote: Though they cause my body to be cut up as small as the very dust, I will never return; and I here take an oath to this.
stops.quote_source: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Samuel Beal, Book I, p. 18
suggested_refs: The Tang Yumen Pass near Guazhou, distinct from the Han ruins west of Dunhuang
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: The first beacon tower, shot at in the dark
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the towers are attested as a system, this episode only through Huili
stops.campa: He reaches the first tower after dark and waits for the moon to set before crawling to the water. An arrow passes his knee; a second nearly hits him. He stands up in the open and calls out what he is. They take him inside by torchlight, and the commander Wang Xiang, a Buddhist, hears the accent of the capital in his speech, feeds him, fills his skins, and sends him on with a letter to the fourth tower, where the commander is his kinsman, and word to go round the fifth altogether, whose officer he calls a hard man.
stops.quote: I am a priest come from the capital: do not shoot me!
stops.quote_source: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal, Book I, p. 19
suggested_refs: The five signal towers west of the Tang Jade Gate
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: The Mohe waste, four nights without water
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the crossing is universally reported, the details are Huili's alone
stops.campa: In the Mohe waste he misses the spring he was told to find, and then spills the whole of his water skin trying to drink from it in the dark. For four nights and five days he goes without water, riding by the bones and the dung of earlier caravans, seeing armies of mounted men in the heat that dissolve when he looks at them. On the fifth night a wind comes cold enough to wake him where he has fallen, and the old red horse turns off the track by itself and walks to grass and a pool.
stops.quote: I made a vow at the first that if I did not succeed in reaching India I would never return a step to the East; what then am I now doing here? It is better to die in the attempt to go to the West, than to live by returning to the East.
stops.quote_source: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal, Book I, p. 22
suggested_refs: The Mo-kia-yen desert crossing, the narrow point of the whole journey
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

segments.name: The Oasis Kingdoms and the Ice Mountain

stops.name: Yiwu, the monks who weep at his accent
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the stop is attested, the month is not
stops.campa: Eighty leagues of waterless ground end at the oasis kingdom of Yiwu, and in its monastery three Chinese monks, one of them an old man who has not seen his country in decades, come out weeping to take hold of him. He rests ten days and eats food cooked the way it is cooked at home. Envoys of Gaochang are in the town and send word across the sand ahead of him. On the tenth day a relay of horses comes back over it, sent by King Qu Wentai with an escort and an instruction to travel by way of Gaochang, which is not on the road he chose.
suggested_refs: Yiwu, modern Hami, first foreign kingdom on the road
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: Gaochang, the king who will not let him go
stops.date_confidence: contradiction in the pool: the Gaochang record and the geography lens give 629, the chronology lens gives 630; the sworn brotherhood and the gifts rest on Huili alone
stops.campa: King Qu Wentai receives him at midnight by candlelight and will not let him leave. He asks him to stay and be teacher of the kingdom for life; Xuanzang refuses and stops eating, sitting upright three days without water until the king gives way. They swear brotherhood before the king's mother. Then Gaochang equips the journey it could not prevent: four novices, twenty-five servants, thirty horses, gold and silver and bolts of satin, and twenty-four letters to the kings of the road west, each with a roll of silk to carry it.
suggested_refs: The Kara-Khoja ruins at Turpan, seat of the Qu dynasty of Gaochang
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: Kucha, snowbound with Moksagupta
stops.date_confidence: attested to the winter of 629 into spring 630; the passes were shut for about two months
stops.campa: Past Yanqi, whose king is cool to him because Gaochang has lately stolen his horses, the road reaches Kucha, the largest Buddhist kingdom of the Tarim rim: a hundred monasteries, five thousand monks, two colossal Buddhas standing outside the western gate. Snow closes the mountains and holds him two months. He debates the aged Moksagupta, who tells him India is not worth the walk and that everything he needs is in the Abhidharma already held here. Xuanzang asks him for texts the old man does not have.
suggested_refs: The Kizil and Subashi cave monasteries near modern Kuqa
sources: Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, book 1
Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: The Ice Mountain, a third of the party lost
stops.date_confidence: the crossing is attested; the pass is named only Ling Shan in Xuanzang's text, and scholars dispute whether it was the Bedel or the Muzart, so the pin is a reconstruction
stops.campa: The Ice Mountain has no dry ground on it for four hundred li. The party climbs among crevasses and hanging ice, cooks in pans set on the ice itself and sleeps on the same ice, and the wind comes down the glacier at night with nothing standing in its way. Seven days of this. When the descent ends, a third of the men who started the pass are dead of cold, guides among them who had crossed it before, and a number of the oxen and horses have gone into the crevasses with their loads and the manuscripts on them.
suggested_refs: The Bedel and Muzart passes of the Tian Shan, rival candidates for Ling Shan
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: Suyab, audience in the tent of gold flowers
stops.date_confidence: the audience is attested; whether the qaghan was Tong Yabghu himself or his son is disputed, since Tong Yabghu died around 628-630 and the identification depends on which departure year is accepted
stops.campa: He comes down along a great salt lake he calls Qingchi, which never freezes though the mountains above it stay white all year, and follows the Chu valley to the camp of the Western Turks. The qaghan is out hunting with a horde of horsemen in brocade. The tent is worked with gold flowers, the drink is wine, the music is not Buddhist. The ruler of the steppe from here to Persia receives the illegal traveler as an honored guest, gives him an interpreter with Chinese and Sanskrit, and writes the letters that carry him to India.
suggested_refs: The Ak-Beshim ruins near Tokmok, site of Suyab
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: Samarkand, the fire temple and the king's reversal
stops.date_confidence: attested to 630; the month is inferred from the march
stops.campa: Samarkand is rich, Zoroastrian, and closed to his religion: two monasteries stand empty and the locals drive off any monk who tries to lodge in them. Two of his novices go in to worship anyway and are chased out with fire. Xuanzang speaks to the king, who had received him coldly, and the king reverses himself, punishes the men, and reopens the houses. Alexander killed Cleitus in this city nine centuries before him, and Genghis Khan will burn it six centuries after. The pilgrim stays a few days and turns south.
suggested_refs: The Afrasiab mound, pre-Mongol Samarkand
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: The Iron Gates, bells hung on the plates
stops.date_confidence: attested as a stage of the route; the day is inferred
stops.campa: The road to Bactria runs through a defile the Turks hold as a border: sheer rock on both sides, a track wide enough for one animal, iron plates hung across the gates and bells fixed to the plates. He records the color of the stone and the sound of the bells. Somewhere in this same broken Sogdian country Alexander stormed the rock fortress where he found Roxana, and the Macedonian garrisons left names on the map that the pilgrim's own book will still be reporting to Chinese readers a thousand years later.
suggested_refs: The Buzgala defile in Surxondaryo, the Iron Gate of the Turks

stops.name: Termez, the Oxus crossing
stops.date_confidence: attested as a stage; the month is inferred
stops.campa: He ferries the Oxus at Termez, where the river runs wide and slow and monasteries stand along both banks, more than ten of them by his count with a thousand monks between them. The country beyond is Tukhara, split among twenty-seven small lords, all of them subject to the Turks. Here the party turns west up the river toward Balkh instead of south, because the great monastery he has been told of is the one place in Central Asia where the texts are said to be complete rather than partial.
suggested_refs: The Buddhist monastic ruins of Kara Tepe and Fayaz Tepe at Termez

stops.name: Balkh, a month at the Nava Vihara
stops.date_confidence: attested to 630; the month is inferred from the sequence
stops.campa: Balkh he calls little Rajagriha, a city of a hundred monasteries and three thousand monks, sacked lately by the Turks and still full of relics: a basin the Buddha used, a tooth, a broom of grass. He stays about a month at the Nava Vihara, the New Monastery, which he judges the finest north of the Hindu Kush, and takes two of its scholars onto his party for the road south. Alexander married Roxana in this city and left a Greek town standing on it. The pilgrim, walking the same streets, is looking for a manuscript.
suggested_refs: The Nava Vihara (Naubahar) monastery mound outside Balkh

stops.name: Bamiyan, the two figures in the cliff
stops.date_confidence: attested to 30 April 630; the Sogdian and Tokharistan stages before it are dated only by sequence, so their months are inferred backwards from this fixed point
stops.campa: He comes over the passes into a valley where the cliff face has been cut into. Two standing Buddhas, the taller gilded and by his estimate a hundred and forty feet, which is an underestimate; a reclining figure in a monastery nearby that no excavation has ever found. He counts ten monasteries and a thousand monks in a kingdom of snow and barley whose king gives away everything he owns and buys it back from the monks. His few sentences are the earliest written description of the statues, and after March 2001 they are among the last.
suggested_refs: The empty niches of the Bamiyan Buddhas, destroyed March 2001
sources: Wikipedia, 'Great Tang Records on the Western Regions'

stops.name: Kapisa, wintering with the king's debate
stops.date_confidence: attested to 630; the winter residence is Huili's
stops.campa: The king of Kapisa, a Buddhist and a Kshatriya, comes out to meet him and asks him to lodge at the royal monastery rather than at the Hinayana houses, since the Chinese monk is Mahayana. A debate is arranged, several schools against each other before the court, and Xuanzang takes part in a language he has been speaking for less than a year. He winters at the royal monastery. In the spring the king gives him an escort for the passes that drop into Lampaka, and pays for it out of his own treasury.
suggested_refs: The Begram ruins, summer capital of Kapisa
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: Lampaka, the point at which India begins
stops.date_confidence: attested as the entry point; the month is inferred. Lampaka and Laghman are the same place, and the west-to-east order runs Kapisa, Lampaka, Nagarahara, Gandhara
stops.campa: Crossing into Lampaka he reckons himself arrived: this is India, the country the books came from, and everything since Chang'an has been the way to it. He finds ten monasteries here and mostly Mahayana monks in them. Beyond lies Nagarahara with the cave where the Buddha is said to have left his shadow on the rock, which he goes to see and reports as faint, visible to some and not to others. He is twenty-eight or twenty-nine years old and has been on the road a little over a year.
suggested_refs: Lampaka (Laghman), reckoned by Xuanzang as the threshold of India

stops.name: Purushapura, the stupa of Kanishka
stops.date_confidence: attested to 630; the month is inferred
stops.campa: At Purushapura, the old Gandharan capital, he finds a thousand monasteries and nearly all of them empty, courtyards under weeds, and outside the city the stupa of Kanishka, which he gives at four hundred feet and calls the tallest tower in India. The Buddha's begging bowl was kept here and has been carried away to Persia. He is walking through a Buddhism that has already become archaeology, and he writes down what still stands precisely enough that the ruins can be found again from his pages.
suggested_refs: Shah-ji-ki-Dheri, the Kanishka stupa mound at Peshawar

stops.name: Uddiyana, fourteen hundred monasteries mostly empty
stops.date_confidence: attested as a stage of the route; the month is inferred
stops.campa: North up the Swat river lies Uddiyana, where he counts fourteen hundred monasteries along both banks, most of them deserted, and eighteen thousand monks where there were once many more. It is the home country of the Vajrayana texts and of practices he does not fully approve of, and he records its stupas, its rock carvings, and its story of the Buddha giving his body to a hawk. In 1955 Giuseppe Tucci will come up this valley with Xuanzang's book in his hand, hunting Uddiyana, and dig at Butkara until he finds it.
suggested_refs: The Butkara stupa at Mingora, excavated by Tucci's Italian mission from 1956

stops.name: Taxila, the measurements that outlive the city
stops.date_confidence: attested to 630-631; the day is inferred
stops.campa: Taxila is a subject province now, governed from Kashmir, its monasteries mostly fallen and its monks few. He walks the ground of the Dharmarajika stupa, raised where a king in a former life is said to have given his head away a thousand times, and notes the distance and bearing of each ruin from the last. Alexander's army came through here and met the naked philosophers. The archaeologists who eventually uncover the city will work from the Chinese monk's measurements rather than from the Greek accounts.
suggested_refs: The Dharmarajika stupa complex at Taxila

stops.name: Kashmir, two years and twenty scribes
stops.date_confidence: attested to roughly 631-633; the month is inferred
stops.campa: The king of Kashmir sends elephants to the border to bring him in, assigns him twenty scribes and five attendants, and for two years he reads. The valley has kept what the plains have lost: the Abhidharma entire, the commentaries of the council held here under Kanishka, masters of logic and of Sanskrit grammar. He studies under the aged Sanghayasas, and the scribes copy out whatever the kingdom holds. He has been gone from Chang'an four years and has not yet reached the monastery he set out for.
suggested_refs: The Harwan monastery area near Srinagar, seat of the Kashmiri Abhidharma tradition
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: Kanyakubja, the first passage through Harsha's capital
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the itinerary between Kashmir and the Gangetic plain is dated only loosely
stops.campa: The road south and east runs through Chinabhukti, Jalandhara, the Kulu valley, Mathura with its twenty monasteries and its processions of images, and across the Ganges to Kanyakubja, capital of Harshavardhana, who rules the north from the Punjab to Bengal. Xuanzang stops three months to study with the monks there and does not meet the king, who is in the field with his army. Then he goes on east into Magadha, toward the towns of the Buddha's own life, which he has so far seen only in Chinese translation.
suggested_refs: Kanauj, capital of Harshavardhana, 606-647

stops.name: Lumbini, the broken pillar of Ashoka
stops.date_confidence: traditional, c. 637-638; the month is inferred
stops.campa: In the Sakya country he finds the garden where the Buddha was born, marked by a pillar Ashoka raised with a horse on top of it, already split across the middle by lightning and lying where it fell. The tank the mother bathed in still holds clear water. The towns around are deserted, the walls down, the monasteries in ruin among villages of a few families. He records the distance and bearing of each site from the last, and the number of monks in each house that still has any.
suggested_refs: The Ashokan pillar at Lumbini, described by Xuanzang as already broken

stops.name: Kusinagara, the wood where the Buddha died
stops.date_confidence: traditional, c. 637-638; the month is inferred
stops.campa: Kusinagara, where the Buddha died between the twin sal trees, is a ruin standing in a wood: brick foundations, a town with almost no inhabitants, a monastery holding a reclining image of the Parinirvana with its head to the north. He notes the stupa Ashoka built, the place where the body was burned, the stream the mourners crossed. He is walking a geography he has read about in Chinese since he was thirteen, and in every case it is further gone than the books said.
suggested_refs: The Mahaparinirvana temple and stupa at Kushinagar

stops.name: Sarnath, fifteen hundred monks in the Deer Park
stops.date_confidence: disputed: the geography lens dates the visit 636-637, Wikipedia's Sarnath article gives about 640, and the pool does not reconcile them
stops.campa: At the Deer Park outside Varanasi, where the first sermon was preached, he finds what the emptied monasteries of Gandhara did not prepare him for: a working house of fifteen hundred monks of the Sammatiya school. An Ashokan stupa over a hundred feet high stands inside the enclosure, and beside it a stone pillar polished bright as jade. He describes the tiers, and the great vihara with its brass image turning the wheel. The Dhamek stupa on that ground will be identified from this passage and no other.
suggested_refs: The Dhamek stupa at Sarnath, identified from Xuanzang's description

stops.name: Bodh Gaya, prostrate at the tree
stops.date_confidence: traditional, c. 637; the month is inferred
stops.campa: He comes to the Bodhi tree, cut down twice by kings and grown back twice, walled around in brick, and to the temple east of it with its great image of the moment of enlightenment. He lays himself flat on the ground and, the biography records, weeps: he has reached the center of the world and he was born a thousand years late and five thousand miles away from it. Swami Vivekananda will make this his last pilgrimage in 1902, to a tree descended from the one Xuanzang is lying under.
suggested_refs: The Mahabodhi Temple and the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya

segments.name: Nalanda, and the Curriculum of Silabhadra

stops.name: Nalanda, received by two hundred monks
stops.date_confidence: attested to 637; the month is inferred
stops.campa: Four senior monks meet him at the edge of the property and two hundred more, with a thousand lay supporters, bring him in with incense and flowers. Nalanda holds several thousand monks in six great blocks, a hundred lecture sessions a day, observatories in the upper storeys and lakes with blue lotus in them. Silabhadra, past a hundred years old and the only man alive holding the whole curriculum, has been waiting for a Chinese student, having been told in a dream to stay alive until one arrived.
suggested_refs: The excavated viharas and chaityas of Nalanda Mahavihara
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: Rajgir, the Vulture Peak above the old capital
stops.date_confidence: traditional; dated only to the Nalanda years
stops.campa: He climbs the ridge above old Rajagriha to the Vulture Peak, where the Lotus Sutra was preached, and finds a brick shrine standing on the summit and the cave where Ananda was disturbed at his meditation. Below lie the bamboo garden, the hot springs, the walls of the abandoned first capital of Magadha. At Nalanda he is given the Indian name Mokshadeva and an elephant to ride, honors kept for very few, and his days go on the Yogacarabhumi, the text whose disagreements drove him out of China.
suggested_refs: Gridhrakuta, the Vulture Peak shrine above Rajgir

stops.name: Kanchipuram, the southern limit of the record
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Records describe the city, but historians dispute whether Xuanzang went in person or wrote from report
stops.campa: The Records give Kanchipuram as capital of the Dravida country, with more than a hundred monasteries, ten thousand monks of the Sthavira school, and the birthplace of the philosopher Dharmapala, whose successor at Nalanda is his own teacher. Monks out of Sri Lanka meet him here and tell him the island is in famine and civil war, so he turns north again rather than take ship. How much of the southern country he saw with his own eyes, and how much he took down from men who had, is argued still.
suggested_refs: Kanchipuram, southern limit of the Great Tang Records

stops.name: Nalanda, one of ten who can expound fifty collections
stops.date_confidence: attested: two separate visits, 637 and 642, totalling around two years at the monastery
stops.campa: He comes back to Nalanda off the roads of the east and the south, and now he lectures instead of attending. Silabhadra sets him to expound the Mahayana against a Hinayana challenger; a thesis is posted and Xuanzang answers it. Of the thousands at the monastery, perhaps ten men can expound fifty collections of sutras and sastras, and the foreigner is counted among the ten. He is asked to stay for good. He has 657 manuscripts assembled and no intention of dying in India.
stops.quote: There are 1000 men who can explain twenty collections of Sutras and Sastras; 500 who can explain thirty collections, and perhaps ten men, including the Master of the Law, who can explain fifty collections. Silabhadra alone has studied and understood the whole number.
stops.quote_source: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal, Book III, p. 112
suggested_refs: The debating courts of Nalanda under Silabhadra
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: Kamarupa, the king who threatens a monastery for a guest
stops.date_confidence: traditional, dated to 642-643 by the sequence; the month is inferred
stops.campa: Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa, far east on the Brahmaputra beyond where Buddhism reaches, sends letter after letter to Nalanda asking for the Chinese monk, and at last threatens to come and take the monastery apart. Silabhadra sends him. The king keeps him a month, questions him about the Tang emperor, and turns out to have heard already, from traders on the Burma road, a song about the campaigns of Taizong. When Harsha demands the guest back, the king brings an army and a fleet up the Ganges to deliver him.
suggested_refs: Kamarupa under Bhaskaravarman, easternmost court of the journey
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: Kanyakubja, the thesis nobody answers
stops.date_confidence: generally dated to about 643 by historians; the sources consulted place it within Harsha's reign of 606-647 without fixing a year
stops.campa: Harsha convenes at Kanyakubja an assembly of eighteen kings, three thousand Mahayana and Hinayana monks, three thousand Brahmins and Jains, and five hundred scholars out of Nalanda. A golden Buddha is carried in procession each day with the king walking beside it dressed as Indra, and Xuanzang's thesis on the Mahayana is posted at the gate for anyone to refute. It stands unanswered. Seven centuries later Ibn Battuta will arrive on this same north Indian plain as a foreign scholar and be made a judge by a sultan.
stops.quote: I come from the great Tang country, and I ask permission to seek for the law (religious books) of Buddha.
stops.quote_source: Xuanzang's answer to King Siladitya (Harsha), Si-Yu-Ki, trans. Samuel Beal (1884), Book V
suggested_refs: The twenty-one-day assembly at Kanauj convened by Harsha

stops.name: Prayaga, the king who gives everything away
stops.date_confidence: traditional, c. 643; the quinquennial assembly is attested, its exact date is not
stops.campa: At the meeting of the Ganges and the Yamuna, Harsha holds the almsgiving he holds every five years, seventy-five days of it, and empties his treasury: gold, cloth, jewels, food, the accumulated surplus of an empire handed out to monks and Brahmins and the poor until the king stands there in a borrowed robe owning nothing. Xuanzang watches the whole distribution and writes it down. Then he asks leave to go home, and the king, who has offered him a province's revenue to stay, gives him an elephant and an escort.
suggested_refs: The quinquennial almsgiving of Harsha at the Prayaga confluence
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

segments.name: The Road Home and the Great Wild Goose Pagoda

stops.name: The Pamir, bandits and a river ford
stops.date_confidence: the return crossing is attested; the sources give no stop-by-stop itinerary for the homeward leg, so date and pin are reconstruction
stops.campa: The homeward road climbs into the Pamir, where he records a valley a thousand li long lying between snow ranges with a lake at the middle of it, dark and deep, holding dragons and fish and turtles, and a wind that does not stop. Bandits take part of his baggage in the mountains, and a load of manuscripts goes into a river at a ford along with the elephant carrying it. Six centuries later Marco Polo will cross this same high country the other way and count forty days without a house.
suggested_refs: The Pamir plateau and the dragon lake of the Great Tang Records

stops.name: Khotan, the letter to the emperor he disobeyed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Huili gives a stay of seven or eight months at Khotan, the month of arrival is inferred
stops.campa: At Khotan, on the southern rim of the Taklamakan, he stops seven or eight months. The lost sutras have to be copied out again from Kucha and Kashgar and he waits for the copies. From here he writes to the emperor whose edict he broke sixteen years before, reporting what he is bringing and asking leave to come home, and sends the letter east with a young trader traveling with a caravan. Marco Polo will find the jade rivers of this oasis still being worked when he passes through in 1273.
suggested_refs: The Yotkan ruins at Khotan, and the jade rivers Marco Polo describes
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: Chang'an, the return of the fugitive
stops.date_confidence: attested to 645; the month of the entry is not fixed in the sources consulted
stops.campa: He arrives to a reception the city has never organized for a monk: the road lined for miles, the streets too packed for the procession to move, the manuscripts and images carried in on twenty horses, 657 texts in 520 cases with about 150 relics among them. Taizong, preparing a campaign in the east, receives him, questions him a whole day about the western kingdoms, and offers him a ministry. Matteo Ricci will enter Beijing on comparable terms nine centuries later, and will also decline to stop being a priest.
suggested_refs: The 645 entry into Chang'an, described by Huili as filling the streets for miles

stops.name: Hongfu Temple, the bureau and the Records
stops.date_confidence: attested to 645-648 for the Hongfu bureau; the Records were completed in 646
stops.campa: Taizong gives him the Hongfu monastery and whatever staff he names, and Xuanzang assembles a bureau: verifiers of meaning, verifiers of text, copyists, senior monks called in from the provinces. In 646 his disciple Bianji finishes the dictated travelogue, twelve volumes and some hundred and twenty thousand characters on a hundred and ten countries, and it goes to the throne. He will render seventy-four works into Chinese in nineteen years. Twelve centuries on, Max Muller will edit the same textual family into English at Oxford.
suggested_refs: The Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, presented to Taizong in 646
sources: Wikipedia, 'Great Tang Records on the Western Regions'

stops.name: Ci'en Temple, the pagoda raised for the manuscripts
stops.date_confidence: attested to the third year of the Yonghui era, 652; the monastery itself dates only from 648, so it was not the site of the 645 bureau
stops.campa: At Ci'en, the monastery Prince Li Zhi founded for his dead mother, Xuanzang asks for a tower to keep the manuscripts out of the reach of fire, and builds one in the western manner: five storeys, brick over an earthen core, some two hundred feet. Wu Zetian will pull it down in 704 and raise seven storeys in its place. The Nestorian stele that Athanasius Kircher prints and construes in Rome in 1667, as his proof that a foreign faith reached China early, lies buried a few miles from this pagoda's footings.
suggested_refs: The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, rebuilt to seven storeys under Wu Zetian

stops.name: Yuhua Palace, six hundred scrolls and the last winter
stops.date_confidence: the death date of 5 February 664 at age sixty-one is attested; the pin is the Yijun county seat, since the pool's two lenses give coordinates about twenty kilometres apart for the palace and neither matches the site
stops.campa: Gaozong gives him the mountain palace at Yuhua for the last work, the Mahaprajnaparamita in six hundred scrolls, which his own assistants beg him to abridge and which he refuses to abridge. He finishes it in the winter of 663 and tells them he will not translate again. In the first month of the new year he falls crossing an irrigation ditch, takes to his bed, and dies there on the fifth of February at sixty-one. The funeral procession at Chang'an is reported at a million people.
suggested_refs: Yuhua Palace in Yijun county, where the six-hundred-scroll Mahaprajnaparamita was completed
sources: Huili, Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, trans. Beal

stops.name: Xingjiao Temple, the pagoda over the bones
stops.date_confidence: attested to 669 for the reinterment; the first burial on the plain east of Chang'an rests on temple tradition rather than record
stops.campa: Five years after the first burial on the plain east of the capital, crowds at the grave trouble the emperor enough that the remains are moved south to Shaoling Yuan, and a monastery is founded over them with a five-storey pagoda, flanked by smaller pagodas for the disciples Kuiji and Yuance. The Tang stonework survives the destruction of everything around it in the late Qing. In 2014 the site enters the World Heritage list under the Silk Roads, in the Chang'an to Tianshan corridor.
suggested_refs: The Xingjiao Temple pagoda, Xi'an, inscribed by UNESCO in 2014
sources: UNESCO World Heritage List, 'Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor'
